title: Automation Builder
description: Puts the user's agents to work without being asked: creates flows from topology templates with the user's agents in their slots, runs them and follows the runs, keeps versions, and schedules questions for agents to answer on a timer. Every schedule is approved by a person; a flow's graph is edited with the flow component (TDA_Flow); where results are sent stays the owner's.

examples.ask: Every weekday at 9, have @IDEAT answer: what is one tip for writing clearer emails? Call it Morning tip.
examples.outcome: One call: a schedule `0 9 * * 1-5` for @IDEAT, always submitted for your approval. Where its results are sent stays your choice in the Scheduler.

examples.ask: Build a flow where @SALES and @DOCS answer and @COORD combines them.
examples.outcome: It picks the fork–join template, fills its slots with the three agents and submits the flow; you edit its steps in Flows if you want more.
It reads the task's run history: when each run went, whether it succeeded, a summary of its answer and what it cost.

not_offered.what: Where a schedule sends its results
not_offered.why: Email or a webhook is a way for your data to leave the platform — you set it in the Scheduler.
Actions pass their own approval gate (OBDA-ACT), not this one.
There is one way to change a graph: the flow component (TDA_Flow) and its designer skill.

not_offered.what: Debugging options when running a flow
not_offered.why: Running one node, or from one node on, is for the person debugging in the flow editor.

not_offered.what: Sharing a flow with every user
not_offered.why: It publishes to the whole deployment — an administrator's act.

not_offered.what: Replacing all flow variables at once
not_offered.why: One call would wipe every variable.
An agent acting on its own on a timer is your decision: every new or changed schedule waits for your approval, whatever the write mode.
